Stöd till sökandet och identifieringen av försvunna människor från kriget 1992-95 i BiH.
Insatsen handlar om fortsatt stöd till International Commission for Missing Persons (ICMP). Det senaste avtalet mellan Sverige och ICMP slutade den 31 augusti 2019. ICMP har fått direkt stöd från Sverige sedan 2008 (förutom några månader utan medel / avtal). Det totala utbetalda beloppet sedan 2008 uppgår till 56 MSEK. Sverige går in med medel i projektet tillsammans med EU som genom IPA-stöd bidrar med 3 000 000 EUR. Sverige bidrar med 9 000 000 SEK.
ICMP är en mellanstatlig fördragsbaserad organisation som arbetar med regeringar, civilsamhällesorganisationer, rättsliga institutioner, internationella organisationer och andra över hela världen för att ta itu med frågan om människor som har försvunnit till följd av väpnad konflikt, kränkningar av de mänskliga rättigheterna, katastrofer, organiserade brottslighet, oregelbunden migration och andra orsaker. ICMP har arbetat i BiH sedan 1996 med sökning och identifiering av försvunna människor från kriget. Cirka 70% av de saknade personerna i landet har identifierats och nationella institutioners kapacitet har byggts till följd av ICMPs arbete.
Det övergripande målet för projektet är att påskynda övergångsrättvisa genom att hitta och identifiera saknade personer från konflikten 1992-1995. Det specifika målet är att öka det inhemska ägarskapet till processen för försvunna personer och säkerställa kontinuitet i hanteringen av saknade personer. ICMP kommer därför att arbeta med tekniskt bistånd till inhemska myndigheter i sökandet efter försvunna personer och med kapacitetsuppbyggnad av myndigheter och stöd till familjeorganisationer i syfte att överföra ägarskapet kring hanteringen av försvunna personer i Bosnien och Hercegovina.

Support to the search and identification of missing persons from the war in BiH 1992-95.
The contribution is about continued support to the International Commission for Missing Persons (ICMP). The last agreement between Sweden and ICMP ended August 31 2019. ICMP has received direct support from Sweden since 2008 (apart from a few months without funds/agreement). The total amount of disbursed funds since 2008 amounts to 56 MSEK. Sweden will contribute with funds for the project together with EU, who provides 3 000 000 EUR through IPA-funds. Sweden contributes with 9 000 000 SEK.
ICMP is an intergovernmental treaty-based organisation working with governments, civil society organizations, justice institutions, international organizations and others throughout the world to address the issue of people who have gone missing as a result of armed conflict, human rights abuses, disasters, organized crime, irregular migration and other causes. ICMP has worked in BiH since 1996 with the search and identification of missing persons from the war. Around 70 % of the missing persons in the country have been identified and capacities of national institutions have been built as a result of ICMPs work.
The overall objective of the project is to accelerate the transitional justice process by accounting for missing persons from the conflict of 1992-1995. The specific objective is to increase domestic ownership of the missing persons process and to ensure continuity in resolving missing persons issues. Hence, ICMP will work with technical assistance to domestic agencies in the search for missing persons and with capacity building of agencies and support to associations of families of the missing with the aim to transfer ownership of the issue of addressing missing persons in BiH.

description.narrative:
The Embassy assessment of results, is based on the narrative report received at the end of Q1 2025, the public event presenting ICMP-results held in July 2025 and on regular follow up meetings held with ICMP and EU during 2025.
The project continued to make progress through field work and laboratory work - including the forensic laboratory in Tuzla -, the collaboration with national authorities and through the financing of limited activities carried out by the associations of family members.
The expected results include the planned and continued with work with the Integrated Data Management System at the Missing Persons Institute (MPI), which has streamlined data management and improved the efficiency of identification processes. There has been a noticeable increase in field activities and DNA matching efforts, leading to new identifications. These advancements are crucial for providing closure to families of missing persons and enhancing the overall effectiveness of the program. During the reporting period (calendar year 2024), ICMP submitted 261 DNA matching reports to the relevant authorities. These include 70 new identities, 131 re-association reports (where identified body parts belong to already identified victims), 11 exclusions reports and 49 no-name/post-mortem re-associations reports. Possibly one un-expected result could be that the high level of matching reports, places BiH among the leading countries in terms of victim identifications related to war crimes.
The ICMP has provided technical support to BIH authorities, including the Prosecutors Office, the BIH Agency for Forensic Examinations and Expertise (AFEE) and MPI. This support is assessed as absolutely instrumental in building local capacity and ensuring the sustainability and increased national ownership of the project. Training sessions have been conducted for MPI staff on the use of iDMS (identification Data Management System) and DNA laboratory procedures. These programs are essential for maintaining high operational standards and ensuring that staff are well-equipped to handle complex identification tasks.
The support to the Family Associations (FA) has been ongoing during the reporting period. As always the support contributes to the commemoration and preservation of memory of the genocide and the victims. It also contributes to raising public awareness of the issue of missing persons, continuing the discussions with government and legal representatives aiming at legal reforms and stronger actions, connecting and empowering the families, including "marginalized" victims particularly the Roma community in the pursuit of justice, and also to building partnerships and strengthening the dialogue between different actors. The financial support to the FAs' work is not very large, but is considered as vital for many of the organisations. In total 48 000 USD was disbursed to 18 family associations through the small grant scheme managed by ICMP.
Regarding observed weaknesses and challenges, the narrative report has identified delays in the procurement of essential DNA laboratory equipment for the Agency for Forensic Examination and Expertise, which is funded through the EU-contribution to the project. These delays have impacted the expected outputs and slowed down the overall progress of parts of the project. It is expected that the pace will be improved when the equipment is in place. Another identified challenge is the need for better coordination within the Prosecutors Office (PO) to avoid overlapping exhumation dates. Improved planning and communication are necessary to ensure that exhumations are conducted efficiently and without unnecessary delays. ICMP is optimistic regarding possibilities to improve planning and within the PO.
